Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module, server-rendered Spring Boot application for uploading, browsing, viewing, and deleting photos. This assessment reflects the source code, Maven build, application configuration, templates, and Docker Compose deployment.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle stores photo bytes as a LOB and metadata in the photos table, including a UUID string identifier, original filename, MIME type, size, upload timestamp, and optional dimensions. Runtime uploads are stored in the database, not an upload directory or object store. Docker Compose persists database files through oracle_data; the application container has no photo-storage volume. Both default and Docker profiles configure Hibernate schema recreation with ddl-auto=create, so persistent database files do not imply preservation of application tables across application starts. Browser templates load Bootstrap CSS and JavaScript from jsDelivr. No application-level cache, message broker, email service, or external business API integration was identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on the PhotoService interface, its implementation depends on PhotoRepository, and Spring manages transactions around service operations.
  • Photo content and metadata share the Oracle persistence model. Repository queries use Oracle-specific native SQL features, including NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE, and DUAL.
  • Gallery and photo reads are public; upload and delete POST requests require authentication. Security uses a configured in-memory identity with BCrypt, stateless HTTP Basic, and disabled CSRF; sensitive configuration values are externalized.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes five controller-defined HTTP endpoints: two HTML views, a multipart upload returning JSON, a deletion action, and a binary photo response. Requests use synchronous controller-to-service calls and database access; no service-to-service HTTP API or messaging contract was found.

pom.xml defines one executable JAR, not a multi-module build. Key application dependencies are Spring Boot Web, Thymeleaf, Data JPA, Security, Validation, JSON, and the Oracle JDBC driver. docker-compose.yml defines the two services above; no additional deployment services were identified.

Evidence: pom.xml, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and the application resource files.

API Endpoints Inventory

All paths are unversioned. There is no URL, header, or query-based API versioning scheme.

Service / controllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
Application / HomeControllerGET/No required parameters200 HTML rendered from index, using List in the view model. Retrieval errors produce an empty gallery rather than an explicit error status.
Application / HomeControllerPOST/uploadmultipart/form-data; repeated required files parts bound to List; HTTP Basic authentication200 JSON Map containing success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads. Empty input or controller-handled MultipartException: 400 JSON containing success=false and error. Missing authentication: 401.
Application / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}String path parameter id200 HTML rendered from detail, with a Photo and optional previous/next photo identifiers. Missing photo, invalid ID, or retrieval/navigation error: redirect to / (normally 302).
Application / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deleteString path parameter id; no request body contract; HTTP Basic authenticationRedirect to / (normally 302) after successful deletion, missing photo, or deletion error; adds a success/error flash attribute. Missing authentication: 401.
Application / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path parameter id; browser may append an ignored cache-busting _t query parameter200 ResponseEntity backed by ByteArrayResource, using the stored media type. Missing photo or empty bytes: 404 with no body. Caught processing/retrieval error: 500 with no body.

Upload item rejection is reported inside the 200 response, including when every submitted file fails; it is not uniformly a 400 response. Files are processed sequentially, and successful items are re-read to build response metadata. A missing required multipart parameter can also be rejected by Spring MVC before handler execution.

Binary photo responses set no-cache headers and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, and X-Photo-Size. Controllers do not define a common error DTO or global error-envelope policy.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/{HomeController,DetailController,PhotoFileController}.java; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js.

There are no gateway-level aggregation DTOs. Jackson supplied through Spring Boot JSON handles map serialization, including timestamps in upload metadata; no custom serializer or serialization override was identified. Thymeleaf renders view-model entities separately from the JSON upload contract.

No OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf schema, GraphQL schema, or associated endpoint implementation was found. For entity fields and persistence mapping, see the companion data-architecture.md; individual validation rules belong in business-workflows.md.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser to application: HTML navigation and form deletion use HTTP; upload JavaScript uses same-origin fetch('/upload') with FormData. JavaScript's async/await is client-side request handling, not asynchronous inter-service messaging. No message broker, event bus, pub/sub, or gRPC usage was found.
  • Inside the application: Controllers directly invoke PhotoService, implemented by PhotoServiceImpl, which calls PhotoRepository. Repository calls use Spring Data JPA and synchronous JDBC communication with Oracle. Detail rendering combines the selected photo and navigation identifiers within one application, not through gateway composition.
  • Resilience and timeouts: No circuit breaker, automatic request retry, bulkhead, or application-defined outbound HTTP timeout was identified. No explicit JDBC connection/read timeout was identified in the reviewed application settings. Browser upload code defines neither an abort timeout nor a retry policy. Compose process restart behavior is not a request retry contract.
  • Fallback behavior: Gallery retrieval errors return an empty HTML gallery; detail errors redirect home; deletion errors also redirect with an error flash attribute. Upload service failures usually become per-file failure entries; errors outside that handling have no custom fallback. Binary photo retrieval errors return 500. No cross-service aggregation fallback exists.
  • Discovery and routing: Compose provides service-name resolution for database connectivity. No Eureka/Consul registration, API gateway, application client-side load balancing, or backend HTTP-service client was found.
  • Availability: Compose orders application startup after database health. Database connectivity and required administrator configuration affect application availability; see configuration-inventory.md for startup/configuration details.
  • API security: SecurityConfig requires authentication for POST /upload and /detail/*/delete, using stateless HTTP Basic and an in-memory administrator account. Read endpoints are public. The configured account has an administrator role, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than a specific role; no method-level authorization was found. CSRF protection is explicitly disabled. No application TLS listener or HTTPS termination service is configured in the inspected deployment, so secure transport must be supplied externally. No JWT or OAuth2 contract was found.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java, controller sources, upload JavaScript, and Compose. No credential values are reproduced here.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Operator-provided environment → Compose interpolation: required Oracle/application/admin passwords must be present before service creation.
  2. oracle-db → Oracle startup and schema initialization: ./oracle-init mounts at /opt/oracle/scripts/startup. Both shell scripts use set -euo pipefail, require password variables, and create the schema if missing. create-user.sh adds a fixed 30-second delay. 02-verify-user.sql checks a fixed masked username, which may not match an overridden APP_USER.
  3. Oracle readiness → application-schema SQL connection: Compose pipes SELECT 1 FROM DUAL; to sqlplus -s using APP_USER/APP_USER_PASSWORD against local Oracle port 1521/service XE. Interval 30s, timeout 10s, retries 15, start period 180s; these are configured probe timings, not a guaranteed startup deadline. The standalone healthcheck.sql is not referenced by this probe.
  4. photoalbum-java-app → waits for → healthy oracle-db: Compose depends_on.oracle-db.condition=service_healthy; app restart policy on-failure. The database credentials/schema and required admin password are startup dependencies.

No config/discovery server, application readiness probe, additional wait utility, Spring Cloud Config retry, or explicit application startup timeout was found. The Oracle health gate is startup ordering, not continuous application dependency supervision.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env, replaces placeholders, and supplies required values → Compose passes the database administrator password and schema credentials into Oracle → startup shell scripts authenticate as Oracle's administrative account and create/configure the application schema → Compose binds the same schema password to Spring datasource settings and injects separate admin credentials into the application.

01-create-user.sh grants schema-creation/session privileges, including table, sequence, view, procedure, trigger, type and synonym creation, and tablespace quota; it deliberately avoids DBA/system-wide ANY grants. The other shell script creates a missing user with session/table/sequence privileges. Neither script updates an existing user's password, so changing environment values alone does not rotate credentials already persisted in oracle_data.

The SQL health probe uses application schema credentials. SecurityConfig BCrypt-encodes the injected application admin password when constructing its in-memory user. This is password hashing, not encryption of .env, configuration files, or container environment values. No managed identity, service principal, RBAC-based external secret access, Key Vault/Vault integration, encrypted properties, sealed secrets, or implemented CI secret-provisioning workflow was found.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse uploaded photographs, inspect individual images, and navigate chronologically through the collection. Authenticated users can add multiple photos and permanently remove photos from the shared gallery.

The sole persisted business entity; no explicit DDD aggregate framework is present.Independent collection item; previous and next photos are derived from upload chronology, not stored relationships. No user ownership or album grouping is modeled.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload processingTransient outcome of processing one candidate photo, not a persisted entity. Communicates acceptance or a reason for rejection.Refers to the newly stored Photo on success; controller combines individual outcomes into batch feedback.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload multiple photos and update the gallery

  1. A user selects or drops files into the gallery. The browser applies Client upload eligibility and submits eligible files together to POST /upload.
  2. The security filter requires authentication before the controller processes this state-changing request.
  3. HomeController applies Batch presence, then invokes PhotoService separately for each file.
  4. PhotoService applies Server upload eligibility and Image inspection. An accepted candidate becomes a Photo with a generated identity and upload time; its content and metadata are saved together.
  5. A rejected candidate yields an unsuccessful UploadResult with a file-specific error. The controller continues processing subsequent files when the service returns a failure result.
  6. For each successful result, the controller reloads the Photo by its new identity and composes a metadata-only response item. If the reload returns no photo, that result is omitted from both response lists; a retrieval exception can instead interrupt the request.
  7. The controller returns accepted-photo metadata and failed-file messages together under Batch outcome.
  8. The browser prepends cards for accepted photos, requests their stored content separately, and displays returned per-file failures. An unsuccessful HTTP response or network error produces generic upload feedback.

This is synchronous controller orchestration, with independent per-file service transactions rather than an all-or-nothing batch. Previously committed files are not compensated if later processing fails.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-132,135-179, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-107, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and inspect adjacent photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController requests the collection and renders gallery cards under Gallery ordering.
  2. If retrieval fails, the controller logs the error and renders an empty collection. The page uses the same “No photos yet” display as a genuinely empty collection; it does not distinguish an outage.
  3. A visitor selects a photo through GET /detail/{id}. DetailController applies Photo lookup and retrieves the chosen photo.
  4. The service derives previous and next photos using Chronological navigation. The detail page shows metadata and only those navigation links for which a neighbor exists.
  5. The browser separately requests image content through GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController applies Content availability and returns the original stored bytes and media type. Images are delivered without reusable browser caching.
  6. A missing photo or any detail-loading failure redirects to the gallery. Missing content returns not found; an unexpected content-serving exception returns a server error, without a substitute image.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-59, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-87, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-113, src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-132.

Workflow 3: Confirm deletion and return to the collection

  1. On a photo detail page, the user selects Delete. The browser asks for confirmation; cancellation prevents submission but is not a server-side business constraint.
  2. Confirmation submits POST /detail/{id}/delete; the security filter requires authentication.
  3. PhotoService looks up the photo under Deletion existence, deletes it when present, and returns a boolean outcome.
  4. DetailController redirects to the gallery with success or not-found feedback. A service exception instead produces retry-oriented failure feedback.
  5. Removal is permanent in the application: there is no recycle bin, undo operation, or compensating recovery workflow.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209.

No scheduled business jobs, event listeners, batch commands, or business-state initialization routines were found in the application source. The application entry point only starts the application (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no remote business-service calls or gateway aggregation endpoints. Composition happens inside the application:

  • Upload feedback: browser files → HomeController → PhotoService → photo database. The controller uses each successful Photo identity to fetch metadata, combines accepted items and rejected-file messages, and returns them to the browser. Binary content is not included in that response.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the chosen Photo with two chronology queries against the same collection. The browser joins that rendered metadata with a separate content request using the Photo identity.
  • Content delivery: PhotoFileController obtains the Photo through the same business service and returns its stored content. The upload workflow does not write new photos to the static upload directory or a remote object service.
  • Degradation: gallery retrieval failure becomes an empty-gallery display; detail retrieval or navigation failure redirects to the gallery; unavailable content produces not-found or server-error responses. Upload processing returns per-file errors where caught, but database failures during transaction completion or subsequent reload can escape that feedback path.

There is no circuit breaker, asynchronous propagation, remote-service fallback, or cached domain snapshot in these flows.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-97, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-177.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and acceptance

  • Client upload eligibility: browser-declared media type must be JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP; each file must be at most 10 MiB. Other candidates are excluded locally. This is a convenience check, not authoritative server validation.
  • Batch presence: an absent or empty file list is rejected as a bad request. HomeController maps multipart exceptions to the same “No files provided” response.
  • Server upload eligibility: compare the lowercased declared content type against the configured allowlist, reject sizes above the configured maximum, and reject empty files. Current application settings allow the same four image types and 10 MiB per file; multipart parsing also limits the overall request to 50 MB. A missing content type reaches the generic unexpected-error handler.
  • Image inspection: read image dimensions from the header where an image reader is available; reject an inspected image exceeding 40,000,000 pixels. File-reading IO errors fail the upload. No available reader or other dimension-extraction exceptions permit continuation without dimensions; this is not a requirement that every upload fully decode as an image.
  • Photo metadata validity: the model declares a nonblank original filename of at most 255 characters, a nonblank media type of at most 50 characters, a positive nonnull file size, and a nonnull upload time. These are model validation constraints rather than controller-level validation of the multipart input.
  • Batch outcome: response success is true only when at least one accepted photo has been reloaded into the response list. Normal processing returns HTTP success even when every file produces a rejection outcome. The configured maximum-files-per-upload value of 10 is not referenced by the controller or service and is not an implemented count limit.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:65-79, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:63-107, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,80-152, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:31-64, upload and multipart settings in src/main/resources/application.properties.

Collection decisions and lifecycle

  • Gallery ordering: collection retrieval sorts newest uploads first. There is no pagination or user-specific filtering in the business service.
  • Chronological navigation: previous means the closest strictly older upload; next means the closest strictly newer upload no later than the database current time. The service takes the first ordered candidate. Equal upload timestamps are not neighbors, and future-dated photos are excluded from the newer-photo query.
  • Photo lookup: blank or absent detail identities, nonexistent photos, and detail-loading errors return visitors to the gallery.
  • Content availability: blank identities, missing photos, or absent/empty stored bytes produce not found. Unexpected retrieval or response-construction errors produce a server error.
  • Deletion existence: missing photos produce a false outcome; existing photos are physically removed.
  • Lifecycle and integrity: accepted photos enter the collection directly, with no draft, moderation, or publication state. Construction generates identity and upload time; rejected candidates are not saved. There is no duplicate-content/filename check, owner relationship, quota, or bidirectional domain relationship maintenance.
  • Computed presentation: image dimensions are optional; gallery cards calculate rounded KiB sizes, while detail views choose bytes, KiB, or MiB according to magnitude. Displayed dates are derived from upload time.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-229, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:78-90, detail and gallery templates.

Cross-cutting business behavior

  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional; retrieval and navigation methods are marked read-only. Each controller-to-service upload call has its own transaction, and the reload is a separate call. The whole batch and the multi-query detail view do not share a controller-level transaction. A caught save exception does not guarantee successful commit or guaranteed delivery of the returned UploadResult if the transaction is rollback-only.
  • Error handling: upload failures use UploadResult rather than custom business exceptions. Retrieval/deletion errors are logged and wrapped as runtime exceptions; controllers translate them into the outcomes described above. No automatic retry, compensation, dead-letter flow, or saga is implemented.
  • Audit and logging: successful uploads and deletions, rejected uploads, and retrieval failures are logged. Content serving additionally logs filenames, content sizes, and a short byte sample. There is no dedicated durable business audit entity or change-history workflow.
  • Authorization: gallery, detail, and content reads are public. Upload and deletion require authentication through HTTP Basic; these routes do not explicitly require an administrator role or check resource ownership. The configured account is assigned an administrator role, but the collection itself is shared. Upload and delete controls remain visible on public pages, so their presence does not imply permission to mutate data.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-28,53-74,164-184,190-229, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72, upload and detail templates.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 3.5.0 is an initial minor-release version; assess supported patch updates before modernization. Java 21 is the declared build target, and Spring Boot 3 uses Jakarta APIs, which matters when integrating older Java EE libraries. Commons IO 2.14.0 is explicitly pinned rather than following parent management and should be reviewed for current maintenance and security fixes. Oracle JDBC compatibility with Java 21 and the target database must be checked once its managed version is resolved. No vulnerability scan or end-of-life verification was performed.

Notable Observations

  • Spring Boot centrally manages all dependencies except the explicitly versioned Commons IO declaration; no lockfile was found among the recognized build/package files.
  • The JSON starter is declared alongside the web starter. Potential transitive overlap is not counted twice here; no resolved dependency graph is available to confirm it.
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope, not runtime or test scope. Optionality controls propagation to consumers; it does not make this a test dependency.
  • The Spring Boot Maven plugin is declared without a version and inherits parent plugin management. Build plugins are separate from application dependencies and excluded from the diagram and totals.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one persistent entity, Photo, accessed through Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. Oracle stores both photo metadata and binary image content; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database.

The context test explicitly activates the test profile (src/test/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplicationTests.java:7-8).
  • Default and Docker startup schema recreation is destructive rather than a versioned migration strategy. Oracle initialization scripts provision/verify the application schema account and permissions; they do not define or seed the photos table.
  • No Flyway/Liquibase dependency, schema migration directory, SQL data seed, or programmatic database seeding was found. The bundled static image is not evidence of database seed data.
  • No custom connection pool or pool sizing is declared. HikariCP is the expected Spring Data JPA auto-configured pool, not an explicitly configured implementation.
  • Connection details are summarized without credentials. See configuration-inventory.md for the full property inventory.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application persistence boundary owns one photos table. Oracle is the runtime store; H2 is a separate, ephemeral test substitute, not a replicated store or additional service-owned database. Photo bytes and metadata are colocated, with no mapped external object store or filesystem persistence relationship.

Controllers access photos through PhotoService, and PhotoServiceImpl accesses PhotoRepository. No other independently deployed data owner, cross-service direct database access, remote data aggregation, shared entity schema, outbox, or event-based synchronization was detected. Reads and writes use the same entity and repository; read-only transaction annotations do not constitute CQRS or a separate read model.
